newsitem.title: USA: Kmart sees $300 mln in cash from sale-leaseback.
newsitem.headline: Kmart sees $300 mln in cash from sale-leaseback.

text.p: Kmart Corp., eager to pay down debt, expects to raise about $300 million in cash from a planned sale-leaseback deal involving about 80 retail properties, a source close to the situation said Friday.

The transaction, which was expected to be valued Friday, will allow Kmart to make significant headway in paying off the remainder of a $1.2 billion term loan taken on last year in a $3.7 billion refinancing package that eased a major debt crisis.
Under the deal, Kmart would sell the store properties, many of which were recently developed, to private investors, then sign long-term leases on the properties, the source said.
The real estate deal is the latest in a string of transactions Kmart has engineered over the past two years to raise cash, including many sales of non-core assets.
A Kmart spokesman declined to discuss the retailer's real estate plans.
On Thursday, Kmart said it would raise $74.25 million by selling its 50 percent stake in a five-store Mexican joint venture, Kmart Mexico.
Although Kmart intends to book a small loss against earnings on the sale, the cash proceeds will used to pay down the term loan, as will the $300 million from the real estate transaction.

Kmart has already paid off more than half of the term loan, and if the retailer can extinguish the rest before June, it will avoid a major increase in interest rates on the loan. Paying the loan off also will eliminate liens that bank lenders have on inventories and certain Kmart real estate.

The term loan was part of a $3.7 billion debt refinancing package that helped to eliminated the threat of Kmart having to pay off up to $3 billion in debt when its credit rating was cut to junk-bond status.

The continued repair of Kmart's balance sheet will help boost investor confidence that company Chairman Floyd Hall and his managment team are following through on their promise to rebuild Kmart's profitability, analysts said.
"Every time you turn around and they do what they say they're going to do, then you gain confidence that they'll turn the business around," said Prudential Securities analyst Wayne Hood.
Hood said Kmart has indicated to analysts that the real estate transaction will bring in about $300 million in cash.
But the major test for Hall's strategy is whether or not Kmart can boost sales and profitability of its core women's and children's apparel lines this year, he added.

Last month, Kmart said it may merge its Builders Square division with Waban Inc.'s HomeBase business in a deal that would create the nation's third largest ome improvement chain, with $4 billion in sales.
The source said, however, that the Builders Square transaction would not help significantly in paying down corporate debt, because it "would bring in only minimal near-term cash flow."
Kmart would, however, benefit from tax credits associated with an expected loss on the Builders Square unit, which is the last of Kmart's remaining specialty retail divisions.
